Hi everyone,

I am an AI systems engineer (not a geometer!) currently experimenting with auto-formalization pipelines. At the suggestion of Prof. Yang-Hui He, I’ve been building an LLM orchestration loop to formalize the baseline geometric statements of the recent Wang-Zahl 2025 proof of the Kakeya Conjecture in ℝ³.

I have successfully formalized the foundational definitions (δ-tubes, intersection bounds) and the ultimate dimH K = 3 theorem statement.
The Engineering Pipeline: Instead of just prompting LLMs, I built a Python diagnostic bridge that intercepts lake build errors and categorizes them to fix Mathlib hallucinations automatically.
The Lean 4 Challenge (MeasureSpace E3): The biggest hurdle the engine had to overcome was that EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3) is wrapped in WithLp 2, which strips away the default measure theory traits of the underlying Pi type. The LLM kept hallucinating that volume would just resolve. To fix this, the engine injected this explicit pullback:

Lean

instance : MeasureSpace E3 where
  volume := Measure.comap WithLp.ofLp volume

My Question for the Community: Since I am approaching this from the ML engineering side rather than the pure math side, I would love any feedback on whether this approach is idiomatic to Mathlib4. Did I handle the WithLp measure space correctly, or is there a more standard Mathlib way to handle Lebesgue measure on Euclidean 3-space?

  • GitHub Repo (Code + Python Engine): https://github.com/Avshrek/KakeyaAutoform

  • Basic.lean File: [[https://github.com/Avshrek/KakeyaAutoform/blob/main/KakeyaAutoform/Basic.lean](https://www.google.com/search?q=https://github.com/Avshrek/KakeyaAutoform/blob/main/KakeyaAutoform/Basic.lean)](https://github.com/Avshrek/KakeyaAutoform/blob/main/KakeyaAutoform/Basic.lean)

Thanks in advance for any insights!

Abhishek Chaturvedi said:

The LLM kept hallucinating that volume would just resolve.

It does just resolve:

import Mathlib

open MeasureTheory

noncomputable example : Measure (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3)) :=
  volume -- works fine

I think your issue is that you are not importing enough
Your second link appears to be broken

@Eric Wieser Ah, that explains it! My LLM pipeline tries to minimize imports to keep build times down, so it didn't have the full MeasureTheory context. Instead of just importing more of Mathlib, it decided to hallucinate that crazy Measure.comap workaround. Thanks for catching that—definitely a blind spot I need to fix in my diagnostic script!

@Yan Yablonovskiy UA Sorry about that! Here’s the working link: https://github.com/Avshrek/KakeyaAutoform/blob/main/KakeyaAutoform/Basic.lean

My LLM pipeline tries to minimize imports to keep build times down

This is probably not a good idea. So long as you start with lake exe cache get, the build time should be at most 10s, and if you use a running lean server then you can avoid paying this cost after every edit

You may be interested in https://github.com/cameronfreer/lean4-skills/ , however in general auto-formalised LLM code requires considerable manual effort to be in Mathlib, which often needs a human understanding of the math and code to adapt it properly (as things stand right now, this doesn't seem to be viable via prompts alone).

@Yan Yablonovskiy UA Thanks for the link! I completely agree—zero-shot prompts fail hard on Lean's typeclass hierarchies, and expecting PR-ready Mathlib code from prompts alone is totally unrealistic right now.

That’s exactly why I built this. I’m treating this as a systems engineering problem. I built a Python diagnostic bridge that intercepts those inevitable LLM hallucinations (like missing MeasureSpace implementations), runs them against a fix-database, and programmatically injects the structure the LLM missed. So it's not the LLM solving it alone, it's the automated scaffolding around it!

@Eric Wieser That explains it perfectly! I'm completely new to the Lean ecosystem and was unknowingly trying to compile Mathlib from scratch, which was taking forever. Because of that, my pipeline was aggressively trying to minimize imports. I had no idea lake exe cache get existed.

Knowing that I can just use import Mathlib and rely on the pre-built cache completely changes how I should architect the LLM prompts. Thanks so much for the pointer, that’s exactly the kind of ecosystem blind spot I was hoping to catch here.
Do you happen to be using any LLMs to form your replies here? Just the way you're speaking seems a bit LLM right now.

Keep in mind the repo i linked is about that, so i didn't mean a zero-shot anything, I mean even the way you (and others similarly) currently do it with a pipeline doesn't seem to be a viable way to get Mathlib ready code without significant (manual) changes.

@Yan Yablonovskiy UA Yes, definitely! I am totally new to the Lean ecosystem and the math terminology here (I'm an AI systems engineer), so I've been using an LLM to help me polish my drafts and sound more formal. I didn't want to come across as disrespectful by using the wrong terminology. I'll drop the formal act though—happy to chat directly

@Yan Yablonovskiy UA I agree,
My bar for "success" right now is literally just "can I get the compiler to say Exit Code 0 without a human adding typeclass bridges." I know the Mathlib review standards (style, generality, avoiding repetition) are incredibly high, and an LLM pipeline spits out code that is nowhere near PR-ready.

You're totally right—a human expert would have to completely rewrite this before it ever touched Mathlib. I'm just playing around with orchestration to see if we can at least automate the initial compilation step

Yea i was just replying to your original posts which asks how this type of thing could fit within Mathlib.
AI can currently make successfully compiling pipelines, although the definitions must be checked.

Please don't reply with LLMs if you can avoid it. I believe this may also be against the guidelines of this forum.
@Yan Yablonovskiy 🇺🇦 Okay, Thankyou for taking time to check out the repo and for the feedback

https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/blob/main/FormalConjectures/Wikipedia/Kakeya.lean
